This page will collect short essays, research notes, teaching reflections, and occasional writing for students, founders, and scholars interested in entrepreneurship, strategy, and venture development.





I will use this space for short pieces on entrepreneurial strategy, startup development, venture financing, strategic thinking, and lessons from teaching entrepreneurship.






I also plan to use this page to share occasional notes for former students who want to stay connected with entrepreneurship, strategy, and career development.






Selected datasets, project writeups, and research resources may be added here over time.

text:
My research advances a sequencing perspective on entrepreneurial development: founders exercise discretion over when strategic activities occur relative to one another, and this sequencing is a source of performance heterogeneity

Strategic Delay examines whether founders exercise discretion over when to accept venture capital and the relationship between the timing of entry and venture development. I introduce a risk-adjusted measure of delay. Startups that appear to delay strategically seem to enter venture capital in a more developed state, engage in less post-financing repositioning, and face a tradeoff between exit quality and acquisition likelihood.

Working Paper
Manuscript available on request.


Abstract


Product–market fit is widely viewed as a defining milestone for startups. Before product–market fit, startups face substantial uncertainty about customer needs, product design, and whether the proposed product creates value for a specific customer segment. After product–market fit, startups can begin shifting from search toward growth. To resolve this uncertainty, entrepreneurs engage in iterative learning before scale-up. Yet, high-growth startups often raise venture capital before product–market uncertainty has been resolved. Despite the prevalence of this sequence, there is limited understanding about how product–market search relates to the sequencing of customer and investor validation. Does obtaining venture capital before customer validation matter for the path to product–market fit? I examine this question by studying the temporal ordering of product–market fit and first venture capital financing. I conceptualize product–market fit as a customer-validated learning milestone and develop a scalable measure using longitudinal enterprise customer-user reviews from a proprietary, global business software review platform. Linking these data to firm-level information on first VC timing and strategic delay among U.S.-headquartered, single-product startups founded between 2010 and 2024, I show that validation sequence is associated with the duration of product–market search. Among firms that attain product–market fit, startups that raise venture capital before product–market fit remain in product–market search substantially longer—approximately three additional years—relative to firms that validate customers before venture financing. I further show that strategic-delay firms are significantly more likely to reach product–market fit before, or in the same year as, first venture capital financing. These results are robust to multiple specifications and alternative definitions of product–market fit attainment. The findings suggest that while venture capital can accelerate development, it may also change the conditions under which iterative learning proceeds; conversely, discretion over the timing of venture capital entry may allow customer validation to occur before external financing. By bringing customer validation and investor validation into the same temporal frame, the paper shows that startup development depends not only on whether ventures learn under uncertainty, but also on when external capital enters relative to the validation of that learning.

title: Strategic Delay
text:
Job Market Paper




Paper available on request. Please email me.




Abstract


This paper reframes venture capital as an external commitment that changes how entrepreneurial firms learn, revise strategy, and scale. But do founders exercise discretion over the timing of this commitment? Can we observe evidence consistent with such discretion at scale, and does delayed entry affect startups’ developmental path and performance? To study these questions, I introduce a risk-adjusted measure of strategic delay, defined as the deviation between a firm’s realized time to first venture financing and its expected timing given observable characteristics, estimated over a broad population of venture-backed and non-venture-backed U.S. startups founded between 1990 and 2020, with outcomes observed through 2024. I further distinguish, among delayed firms, those exhibiting substantial pre-financing organizational building from those whose timing may instead reflect financing frictions. I document a distinct developmental path among strategically delayed firms: they enter venture capital in a more developed state and engage in less post-financing repositioning, particularly fewer large corrective shifts — consistent with founders resolving more uncertainty before external commitment. This pattern is strongest in industries where prior cohorts historically required more post-financing adjustment, suggesting that delay matters most when pre-financing learning is especially valuable. A survey of venture-backed founders corroborates both the measure and the mechanism: founders who report intentionally postponing financing exhibit exhibit deviations from expected timing roughly twice as large as those who do not, and and cite deliberate, strategic reasons for doing so. The descriptive patterns reveal a tradeoff: strategically delayed firms achieve higher exit quality conditional on exit and are less likely to be acquired, without accelerating post-financing scale. A shift-share instrumental-variables design, exploiting exposure-weighted shocks to early-stage venture supply, corroborates the direction of these effects. Together, the evidence indicates that strategic delay reflects a distinct path of venture development in which founders shift learning before external commitment and enter venture capital in a more developed state.

title: Ndu Ugwuanyi
text:
My agenda revolves around one central question: how strategic thinking works — how strategists sequence consequential decisions under uncertainty, and how that capacity is developed.

My agenda rests on a simple conviction: strategy is not only about choosing what to do, but about knowing what to do first, what to defer, what to preserve, and when to commit. It is a skill exercised over time, and one that can be strengthened.
This leads me to two broad problems.


The first is to understand how strategists use sequencing to navigate consequential decisions under uncertainty. Firms, entrepreneurs, investors, and competitors rarely make all choices at once. They stage commitments, delay certain moves, accelerate others, experiment, reposition, and preserve optionality until better information arrives.
My research asks: when does this kind of sequencing improve performance, and when does it fail? When is delay strategic rather than merely passive? When does early commitment create advantage, and when does it lock firms into the wrong path? More broadly, how do strategists use the ordering of decisions to shape outcomes when the future is uncertain?



The second is to understand how strategy education can translate into better strategic thinking among students of business. I view this as a problem of strengthening critical thinking: helping students move beyond the memorization of frameworks toward the disciplined practice of reasoning through complex strategic situations.
This problem has become even more important in the age of AI. As analytical tools become more powerful and more widely available, the distinctive value of business education will depend increasingly on whether students can ask better questions, structure ambiguous problems, evaluate tradeoffs, and make thoughtful judgments under uncertainty.



First, I use large-scale data on startups to examine how young firms sequence developmental milestones such as financing, customer validation, adaptation, and growth. Startups provide a salient empirical setting because early strategic choices are made under severe uncertainty, resource constraints, and shifting external evaluation, and because the ordering of these choices is consequential, and increasingly observable at scale through new data.
Second, I develop pedagogical approaches that bring strategic reasoning into the classroom. My goal is to design teaching methods that help students practice strategy as a form of disciplined reasoning: identifying the problem, considering alternatives, anticipating responses, sequencing actions, and learning from feedback.

text:
Strategy · Entrepreneurship · Innovation
    Ndu Ugwuanyi
    PhD Candidate, The Wharton School

    
      I study strategic decision-making under uncertainty using entrepreneurial contexts.
    

    
      Job Market Paper
      Research
      CV
    
  




  

    
      I am a doctoral candidate in Strategy and Entrepreneurship at the Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania. My research examines strategic decision-making under uncertainty, with a particular focus on venture development, product-market learning, and the commercialization of emerging technologies.
    


  
      My interest in strategy began well before graduate school. As a teenager, I helped manage a family business in a competitive market, an experience that gave me an early view of how resource constraints, competitive pressure, and judgment shape firm outcomes. Before my PhD, I co-founded a revenue-generating AI startup with engineers across Canada, the United States, and the Netherlands — an experience that deepened my interest in entrepreneurial experimentation, technology commercialization, and the practical challenges of moving from product ideas to scalable firms.
    

    
      I am on the academic job market. I am especially interested in schools where I can pursue rigorous and ambitious research, contribute to high-quality teaching, and translate academic insights into practice.

title: Ndu Ugwuanyi
text:
I teach strategy and entrepreneurship as disciplines of judgment: learning how to frame ambiguous problems, evaluate tradeoffs, test assumptions, and make decisions when uncertainty, competition, and resource constraints are real.



My teaching experience spans multiple institutions, countries, courses, and student populations. I began teaching before undergraduate school, first in chemistry, mathematics, and physics, and later as a lecturer in Nigeria. I have also taught and supported pre-college, undergraduate, MBA, and executive MBA courses in strategy, entrepreneurship, disruptive strategy, global business, business strategy, and mergers and acquisitions. I’ve had teaching experiences at the University of Toronto, Queen’s University, and the Wharton School. For instance, at Wharton, I served as instructor for MGMT 1010: Introduction to Management and currently serve as instructor for Essentials of Entrepreneurship in the Wharton Global Youth Program.




My teaching philosophy is grounded in a simple premise: strategy is learned best when students are asked to make decisions under uncertainty. The classroom should not only transmit management frameworks; it should train judgment. I want students to leave my courses able to diagnose strategic problems, evaluate tradeoffs, defend decisions, revise their assumptions, and understand how strategy changes when uncertainty, competition, and resource constraints are real.
My approach combines active learning, structured discussion, case analysis and diagnosis, applied exercises, simulations and games. I also connect research to practice. My research becomes a tool to help students reason through real strategic-decision making under uncertainty.
Lastly, I treat disengagement as feedback about my design rather than a flaw in my students. The classroom is a live environment, and when learning is genuinely value-enhancing, students have little reason to switch off—I hold myself to creating those conditions.




The comments below were received unsolicited from students after the course and are presented anonymously.



❮





“I’m reaching out to thank you so much for a very memorable experience in the Essentials of Entrepreneurship program. The couple weeks I spent learning from you have been some of the most inspiring and fascinating experiences I’ve had in any learning environment. I’ve learned so much about product development, building an MVP, market sizing and much more.


I am grateful for the time you spent helping our class understand the material. Your dedication to teaching made such a difference—this experience was the highlight of my summer. The program deepened my understanding of entrepreneurship, and further sparked my passion for creating positive social impact through venture creation.


I hope the rest of your summer is full of well-deserved relaxation. Thank you again for everything you’ve done for us this summer. I feel very lucky to have been your student.”




“One thing that has stayed with me wasn’t a particular concept or case study—it was the atmosphere you created in the classroom. Every time someone shared an idea, whether polished or completely unformed, you found something worth building on. Instead of searching for the ‘right’ answer, you encouraged us to explore our thinking. Thank you for creating a space where curiosity mattered more than certainty. It’s a rare quality in a teacher, and one I genuinely appreciated.”




“Hope you’re doing well. I wanted to share an update on what I’ve been up to recently.


I recently competed in the Diamond Challenge with a venture called Medlas AI: a real-time medication verification system for senior living facilities. We made it to the final round at the Limitless World Summit, pitched twice, and while we didn’t take home a top prize, we walked away with a recognition award.


I just wanted to say that your class and teaching style gave me a stronger foundation going into my pitches. Your breakdown of strategy and leadership stuck with me more than I realized.”




“I wanted to message you about how grateful I am for your instruction during my time in the program. I loved hearing your insight on the inner workings of a business. Thank you so much for taking the time and effort to help us grow! It means a lot to me.”




“Thank you for such an inspiring and engaging experience, as the course really deepened my passion for entrepreneurship and helped me think more critically about real-world problem-solving.”




“Your energy and willingness to challenge the group helped us grow, and it’s already changing the way I see business and leadership.”




“I now have a much stronger conceptual foundation for approaching entrepreneurship, and I sincerely hope to share what I learned through this program with my peers in my local community.”





❯
